description: Somos un equipo de 5 estudiantes franceses de la Alianza Francesa de Vitacura, de I° y II° Medio. Creemos que a través del software y de los videojuegos educativos se puede educar a las próximas generaciones sobre la importancia de la exploración espacial y aprenderles las competencias intelectuales necesarias.
summary:
Destination Mars is a browser-based pixel-art game that lets children aged 7–12 explore Mars and build a functioning outpost. Players collect materials, construct infrastructure, connect electricity and resource networks, and manage their astronaut’s oxygen, water and food.

The game addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning engineering trade-offs into practical decisions. Solar panels generate electricity during daylight, but batteries must support nighttime operations. Producing oxygen requires both electricity and water, creating competition for limited supplies. Automated excavators help gather materials but require construction resources, charging and repairs. Players can protect solar panels from meteor showers by folding them, sacrificing electricity generation.

An interactive tutorial, visual resource gauges and English, French and Spanish interfaces make these connected systems approachable. Scientific explanations reference NASA resources on life support and the Martian environment, while accelerated timings and fictional hazards are identified as gameplay simplifications.

By making resource dependencies visible and consequential, Destination Mars helps young learners understand why successful space missions require planning, maintenance and difficult choices.
details:
Destination Mars is a playable browser game that invites children aged 7–12 to become the astronaut, engineer and mission planner of a small Martian outpost. Through exploration, construction and resource management, players discover that survival depends on connected systems: oxygen production needs water and electricity, machines need power, and supplies only help when they are available where they are needed.

Our goal is to make the engineering decisions behind a space mission understandable through play. Players can experiment, observe consequences and improve their strategy, while an interactive tutorial introduces the systems in manageable groups.

How the game works

A new mission begins with an animated landing on a procedurally generated Martian landscape. The lander contains the initial supplies, and the player explores six connected areas to gather materials and expand the outpost. Terrain and mission progress are saved in the browser, allowing players to return to the same colony.

Players construct solar panels, batteries, oxygen generators, tanks, water pumps, greenhouses, storage buildings and habitats. These structures have distinct functions, construction costs and local reserves. Electricity, oxygen and water travel through separate networks of cables and pipes.

Resources are physically distributed. The astronaut carries a limited backpack, a personal oxygen supply, food and a water flask. Supplies stored in a distant building are not automatically available to the astronaut. Players must transport materials, collect provisions and return to suitable infrastructure to refill their suit and flask.

Water pumps extract water from finite ice deposits. Oxygen generators consume water and electricity to produce oxygen, while greenhouses use electricity to grow food. Solar panels produce power during daylight, making batteries important for continued operation at night.

Players can also manufacture autonomous excavators and program them to collect regolith or sulfur. The machines navigate the map, gather materials, return to storage, unload and recharge from its connected electrical network. Automation reduces manual collection, but introduces its own costs, power demand and maintenance needs.

Learning through trade-offs

The central educational mechanic is that useful actions consume something valuable.

For example, a player may have enough electricity to operate equipment during the day but insufficient storage for the night. Expanding food production increases electrical demand. Oxygen production supports exploration, but also draws on water reserves that must be replenished.

Exploration creates another decision: travelling farther can reveal useful resources, but the astronaut must retain enough oxygen, drinking water and provisions for the journey home.

The game also includes fictional, accelerated hazard scenarios. Meteor showers can damage deployed solar panels, while folding panels protects them at the cost of electricity generation. Other events threaten exposed excavators, encouraging players to recall machines or accept the risk of damage. Repairs require carried materials.

Before sleeping through the night, players can consult an uncertain forecast. Forecasts can miss events or raise false alarms, so preparation involves judging risk rather than following a guaranteed prediction. Sleeping advances resource consumption and equipment activity; a report explains what happened during the skipped time.

These mechanics make consequences visible. A shortage is connected to an understandable decision, helping players develop a mental model of how an outpost works.

Accessibility and intended impact

We designed Destination Mars for a low barrier to entry: it runs in a browser without requiring an account or a game installation.

The interface uses pixel-art symbols, resource gauges and contextual controls. An optional interactive tutorial groups related actions into a small number of chapters, introduces systems gradually and pauses simulation time during planning sections. Players can skip the guide entirely.

The game supports English, French and Spanish, including its tutorial and interface. Browser saves allow learners to continue experimenting across multiple sessions.

Our intended impact is to encourage systems thinking, planning and curiosity about space exploration. We want players to understand that producing oxygen, storing energy and maintaining equipment are interconnected responsibilities. The game can also provide a starting point for conversations with parents or teachers about which constraints reflect real engineering and which have been simplified for play.

Scientific grounding and its limits

We referenced NASA educational and technical material when explaining the underlying concepts:

  • Environmental Control and Life Support Systems informed explanations of oxygen production through water electrolysis.
  • NASA’s discussion of solar storms at Mars and Martian dust-storm physics helped distinguish real environmental concerns from fictional effects.
  • NASA Mars24 documentation is referenced for Martian time concepts.

The prototype uses simplified resource units, accelerated days and gameplay-balanced production rates. It does not ingest live NASA data or use DONKI or OSDR datasets. Frequent eruptions, predictable meteor showers and effects that lift vehicles are fictional gameplay scenarios, rather than claims about actual Martian conditions.

Tools and development approach

We built the game using JavaScript, HTML5, and Phaser 4.2.1, with no additional application framework or build system. Maps and save data use JSON, and browser localStorage provides persistence.

The simulation is separated from rendering and advances in fixed time steps. This keeps resource calculations independent of rendering frame rate and allows the same logic to run during ordinary play or a nighttime time skip.

Our team worked in Visual Studio Code, with Git and GitHub for version control and releases. Pixel-art assets included Chipico exports, team-provided artwork and assets. Codex assisted with programming, integration, debugging and documentation.

What makes the project creative

Destination Mars combines direct astronaut exploration with an outpost simulation whose resources remain local. Players experience infrastructure from both perspectives: planning a network and personally depending on it.

Its creativity comes from connecting small, understandable actions into larger consequences. A cable can enable a pump; the pump supplies water; water and electricity enable oxygen production; oxygen makes further exploration possible. The player builds that chain and then lives with its strengths and weaknesses.

Throughout the hackathon, we balanced educational clarity, scientific honesty, accessibility and the need to deliver a working prototype. We prioritized visible dependencies and meaningful decisions, while keeping the simulation simple enough for young players to explore.
